description-meta: "Research lines of the Biodiversity Synthesis Lab (UFMS): metacommunity ecology, eco-evolutionary dynamics, phenotypic evolution of Neotropical species, tadpole morphology, and quantitative methods."
subtitle: "Causes and consequences of species diversity, from ponds to continents"
toc: true

We study what regulates the distribution, composition and diversity of
species across spatial scales, and how the evolution of species' traits feeds
back into those patterns. Most of our work uses **frogs and their tadpoles**
as model organisms, in freshwater systems, along urbanisation gradients and
across biogeographical regions, but we also work with bats, fishes, birds and
arachnids through collaborations. We look not only at the taxonomic but also
at the **functional and phylogenetic** dimensions of diversity, and we treat
the statistical methods behind this work as a research line in its own right.

## Metacommunity ecology across spatial scales

![Frog ponds sampled monthly for three years at a peri-urban site in Campo Grande, central Brazil. From Severgnini et al. (2024), *Ecology and Evolution*, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](assets/images/research/severgnini2024-ponds.jpg){fig-alt="Satellite map of a peri-urban landscape with five ponds outlined in yellow, and inset maps locating the site in Campo Grande, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil"}

We want to understand what regulates species distribution, composition and
diversity in metacommunities at multiple spatial scales: how environmental
gradients, dispersal and evolutionary history combine to assemble local
communities, and how these processes shift over time and space. Our work ranges
from temporal dynamics of frog communities in single ponds to the assembly of
frog faunas on islands worldwide and the delimitation of zoogeographical
regions in the Atlantic Forest. Passive acoustic monitoring is now extending
this work to the Pantanal.

**Key papers**

- Rebouças et al. 2026. [Environmental and geomorphological drivers of frog diversity on islands worldwide](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecog.07818). *Ecography.*
- da Silva et al. 2024. [Zoogeographical regions in the Atlantic Forest: patterns and potential drivers](https://doi.org/10.1111/jbi.14859). *Journal of Biogeography.*
- Severgnini et al. 2024. [Temporal dynamics of species richness and composition in a peri-urban tropical frog community in central Brazil](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.70628). *Ecology and Evolution.*
- Ceron et al. 2022. [Differences in prey availability across space and time lead to interaction rewiring and reshape a predator–prey metaweb](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.3716). *Ecology.*
- Gomes-Mello et al. 2021. [Frog community composition–environment relationships vary over time: are snapshot studies of metacommunity dynamics useful?](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.baae.2021.07.006) *Basic and Applied Ecology.*

**People:** Daiene L. Hokama Sousa, Bruna M. P. Campos; alumni Philip T. Soares,
Gabriel Tirintan and Daniel Din Negri. See [People](people.qmd).

**Funding:** [FrogNet](projects.qmd#frognet-acoustic-monitoring-of-frogs)
(collaboration).

## Eco-evolutionary dynamics in metacommunity ecology

![Phenotypic trajectories of somatic indices across age classes in rural and urban populations of *Leptodactylus podicipinus*. From Franco-Belussi et al. (2024), *Conservation Physiology*, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](assets/images/research/franco-belussi2024-trajectories.jpg){fig-alt="Ordination diagram with arrows connecting young, middle-aged and old frogs; the urban trajectory is long and steep, the rural one short"}

Ecological communities are shaped by a variety of processes that operate at
distinct temporal scales. There is now compelling evidence that evolution by
natural selection can happen in a relatively short time. These
**eco-evolutionary feedbacks** could potentially change species interactions
and further influence evolutionary trajectories.

Cities and agricultural landscapes are our natural experiments: they change
the environment quickly and over large areas. We ask how frog populations
respond to urbanisation and land use, in their physiology, life history and
morphology, and how those responses scale up to community composition.

**Key papers**

- Franco-Belussi et al. 2024. [Multiple morphophysiological responses of a tropical frog to urbanization conform to the pace-of-life syndrome](https://doi.org/10.1093/conphys/coad106). *Conservation Physiology.*
- Sánchez-Domene et al. 2022. [Combined effects of landscape composition and agrochemicals on frog communities amid sugarcane-dominated agroecosystems](https://doi.org/10.1002/eap.2781). *Ecological Applications.*
- Ganci et al. 2021. [High species turnover shapes anuran community composition in ponds along an urban-rural gradient](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11252-021-01174-8). *Urban Ecosystems.*
- Valente-Neto et al. 2021. [Loss of cultural and functional diversity associated with birds across the urbanization gradient in a tropical city](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2021.615797). *Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.*

**People:** Ana Paula Andreazzi, João Victor Santos Barros; alumni Marcos R.
Severgnini and Leandro B. Menezes. See [People](people.qmd).

**Funding:** [FUNDECT/CNPq research productivity grant](projects.qmd#reconciling-phenotypic-evolution-with-metacommunity-theory)
(2024–2027); [CNPq Universal](projects.qmd#eco-evolutionary-dynamics-of-urban-biodiversity)
(2022–2026, completed).

## Phenotypic evolution and diversification of Neotropical species

![Graphical abstract of Bovo et al. (2023), *Integrative Organismal Biology*, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/): thermal tolerance and water balance of frogs along altitudinal gradients in the Atlantic Forest.](assets/images/research/bovo2023-graphical-abstract.jpg){fig-alt="Diagram of frogs and toads climbing a mountain silhouette, with boxes for thermal tolerance, thermal stress and water balance traits"}

Biological diversity is expressed in various ways. One of these is how species
differ from each other. Species' traits may have themselves complex
evolutionary histories, and in turn can influence species distribution,
interspecific interactions, speciation rates, and coexistence.

We're interested in unveiling the patterns of phenotypic evolution in
Neotropical organisms using the toolbox of **modern comparative methods**.
Since species traits can influence diversification patterns, we often
integrate analytical tools and macroevolutionary theory to understand species
distribution at broad spatial scales.

**Key papers**

- Martins et al. 2026. [The impact of climate and habitat on body shape and size evolution in charontid whip spiders](https://doi.org/10.1093/evolut/qpag138). *Evolution.*
- Bovo et al. 2023. [Beyond Janzen's hypothesis: how amphibians that climb tropical mountains respond to climate variation](https://doi.org/10.1093/iob/obad009). *Integrative Organismal Biology.*
- Acero-Murcia et al. 2023. [An evolutionary ecomorphological perspective on the assembly of a Neotropical bat metacommunity](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10914-023-09667-3). *Journal of Mammalian Evolution.*
- Martins et al. 2021. [The evolution of red blood cell shape in fishes](https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.13757). *Journal of Evolutionary Biology.*
- Moroti et al. 2021. [The effects of morphology, phylogeny and prey availability on trophic resource partitioning in an anuran community](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.baae.2020.11.005). *Basic and Applied Ecology.*

**People:** alumni Matheus T. Moroti, Adriana C. Acero-Murcia, Pedro
Abi-Rezik Barros Vianna and Gabriela B. Leite. See [People](people.qmd).

**Funding:** [FUNDECT/CNPq research productivity grant](projects.qmd#reconciling-phenotypic-evolution-with-metacommunity-theory)
(2024–2027); [Humboldt Research Fellowship](projects.qmd#humboldt-sabbatical-at-idiv-20242025)
(2024–2025, completed).

## Evolutionary morphology of Neotropical anuran larvae

![External morphology of the tadpole of *Chiasmocleis altomontana*: (A) lateral, (B) dorsal and (C) oral views. From Menezes et al. (2025), *PeerJ*, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).](assets/images/research/menezes2025-tadpole.jpg){fig-alt="Photographs of a brown tadpole in lateral and dorsal view, and a close-up of its mouth, on a black background"}

The morphological diversity of tadpoles is astonishing. The role of tadpoles
in freshwater ecosystems has been challenged by recent studies using stable
isotopes ([Altig et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2427.2006.01694.x)
*Freshwater Biology*; [Schiesari et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2427.2008.02134.x)
*Freshwater Biology*). Both the **internal and external morphology** of
tadpoles influence habitat use, food acquisition, diet composition, and
several other ecological aspects — including their role in ecosystem
functioning.

Studying the morphology of tadpoles in an evolutionary context can therefore
help us understand community patterns and freshwater ecosystem functioning.
We describe tadpoles of Brazilian species, including their internal oral
features, and maintain the [Brazilian Tadpoles](https://diogoprov.github.io/Brazilian-Tadpoles-5.0/)
online identification reference.

**Key papers**

- Menezes et al. 2025. [The tadpole of *Chiasmocleis altomontana* (Anura: Microhylidae)](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.19220). *PeerJ.*
- Kloh et al. 2023. [Taste for pollen comes in different shapes: consumption by tadpoles from three divergent ecomorphotypes](https://doi.org/10.1111/jzo.13051). *Journal of Zoology.*
- Provete et al. 2021. [The tadpoles and advertisement call of *Trachycephalus imitatrix* and *T. dibernardoi* (Anura: Hylidae)](https://doi.org/10.1670/20-010). *Journal of Herpetology.*

**People:** alumni Leandro B. Menezes and Marcos R. Severgnini. See
[People](people.qmd).

## Quantitative methods and research software

A large part of the work above depends on getting the statistics right for
data that rarely behave like textbook examples — compositional proportions,
multivariate community matrices, phylogenetically non-independent species,
traits measured on very different scales, detections from automated
classifiers that are sometimes wrong. Diogo is an accredited
**Professional Statistician (PStat®)** and **Graduate Statistician (GStat®)**
of the American Statistical Association, and methodological development is
treated here as a research output in its own right, not as a by-product.

Openly available outputs include:

- [**CoDa Stereo**](software.qmd#coda-stereo) brings Aitchison geometry to
  stereological and histomorphometric data, where measurements are
  proportions of a whole and therefore cannot be analysed with off-the-shelf
  parametric tools. It is registered with the Brazilian National Institute of
  Industrial Property (INPI, **BR512026003293-8**) and released under the MIT
  licence, and accompanies a methodological paper currently in review.
- [**crywolf**](software.qmd#crywolf) fits Bayesian occupancy models that
  correct for the false positives of automated detectors, and the
  [**BirdNET Validation Sampler**](software.qmd#birdnet-validation-sampler)
  produces the verified detections those models need.
- [**ecodados**](software.qmd#ecodados) is the R package behind
  [*Análises Ecológicas no R*](https://analises-ecologicas.com), an open
  640-page textbook on ecological data analysis, and
  [**amphiBR**](software.qmd#amphibr) turns the official list of Brazilian
  amphibians into an R dataset.

The same commitment shows up in how we publish and teach. Diogo co-authored
an editorial proposing minimum standards for data and code in ecology and
evolution ([Jenkins et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9961),
*Ecology and Evolution*); course materials
are written in Quarto, versioned on GitHub, and built around real published
datasets rather than simulated ones, so that students meet the problems that
actual data bring with them. See [Software](software.qmd) and
[Teaching](teaching.qmd).

The full list of papers is on the [Publications](publications.qmd) page.
